p.x:
My name is Ton and I am ten years old. When I grow up, I want to be an astronaut. I want to fly in a rocket and see the Earth from space. People say the Earth is round and blue, and I want to see it with my own eyes.
At night, I like to look at the stars. They shine very brightly when there are no clouds. My dad has a small telescope, and we sometimes look at the Moon. You can see the craters on it! Last month, we saw a meteor shower. It was amazing.
I know that space is huge and other planets are very far away. The distance to Mars is millions of kilometres! Astronauts need oxygen because there is no air in space. I also want to explore other planets and land on Mars. Maybe I will meet an alien! My teacher says I must study hard, especially science and maths.

About 400 kilometres above the Earth, the International Space Station (ISS) travels in orbit around our planet. It moves at 28,000 km/h, so the astronauts on board see the sun rise and set sixteen times a day!
Life on the ISS is very different from life on Earth. Because the astronauts are weightless, they float around the station. They sleep in sleeping bags attached to the wall, and they must exercise for two hours every day to keep their muscles strong.
Each mission usually lasts about six months. The astronauts do scientific experiments, repair equipment and sometimes go on a spacewalk outside the station. They also take photographs of the Earth, showing its thin blue atmosphere.
Food and supplies arrive by spacecraft from Earth. Many astronauts say that the best part of the job is looking out of the window. From space, you can't see borders between countries. As one astronaut said, "It made me realise how small and fragile our planet is in the solar system, and in our galaxy."

For most of the twentieth century, space exploration was dominated by governments, most famously during the race between the USA and the Soviet Union that ended with the lunar landings of 1969. Today, a new space race is under way, but this time private companies are leading it.
Commercial firms now launch satellites, deliver payloads to the space station and even sell tickets to tourists. Reusable rockets, which land vertically after launch, have dramatically reduced costs. Some entrepreneurs speak openly of plans to colonise Mars within decades.
The challenges, however, are enormous. Mars has a thin atmosphere, freezing temperatures and dangerous levels of cosmic radiation. Even reaching it requires precise calculation of the spacecraft's trajectory, and current propulsion systems mean the journey takes around seven months. Some scientists have proposed ways to terraform the planet, making it more habitable, but such projects would take centuries.
There are also problems closer to home. Thousands of satellites now orbit the Earth, and pieces of debris from old missions travel at high speed, threatening functioning equipment. Critics argue that the space industry needs international rules before it becomes a dangerous and unregulated venture.
Meanwhile, telescopes continue to discover planets around distant stars, some only a few dozen light years away. The search for extraterrestrial life, once science fiction, is now a serious field of research. Whether or not we find it, the asteroid belt, the comets and the galaxies beyond suggest that the universe still has much to teach us.
